why: A over-reads Washwell's higher margin as higher profit, D over-reads vehicle cost shares of revenue as amounts, and C (prices) is the one statement without basis that sourceHas lists; no slip makes B true by accident.
Option C (B, A, D, C) follows no slip or pair of slips: it is neither the profit order, the shop-count order, the inverted ratio (D, B, C, A) nor the reverse of the answer.

$245 is classes 3 to 5 alone (forgetting classes 1 and 2) and the options form a tight $28 grid (about 9% of the answer), so $273 and $329 are where rough estimates land; no tested slip (swapped percentages, 2011 base, wrong bars) gives $301.

A reverses the sign of the answer, D charges the extra 25c on all 400,000 trays (ignoring the tier and the 10% volume rise), and C counts the 40,000 extra trays at $2.50 (using $1.50 throughout and forgetting the $2.00 per-tray costs); no single slip gives a $55,000 fall.

The options are the four prices tested; the slips that still pick €2.4 (food sales taken as profit, the industry's 15% margin) are both named in sourceHas, while ignoring food (€2.8) or cups per week (€2.0) moves the answer.

A is a near miss (17% rise against 15% fall), B reads the 10% margin fall as a profit fall, D is the one statement without basis sourceHas lists, and reading revenue as profit (which still makes C true) is named in sourceHas.

5% forgets that driver fees grow with revenue, 18% takes the rise as a share of the new revenue (or divides the 5% loss by 27%), and 27% sets the extra revenue equal to the whole depot cost while also forgetting the fees on it; no slip lands on 23%.
B applies the exhibition-visitor share to all visitors (wrong base), C is a near-miss figure from rounding 22% × 26% (5.7%) up to 6%, and D is the one statement without basis sourceHas lists.

5.0 forgets to average over the three years, 0.2 reads the fruit juice series and divides by four, and 0.6 continues the steady ×3 grid; the slips that still land near 1.6 (counting four years, starting in 2009) are not within 20% of it, and both are named in sourceHas anyway.

A (52%) leaves medical equipment out of clinical (58 ÷ 111), and C and D are near misses (9.0% and 27.9%) that look right if the $111m total is rounded to $100m; dividing IT by the total instead (4.5%) makes B false.
